No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends any targeted therapy for ACACB (acetyl-CoA carboxylase 2 / ACC2) alterations, and no oncology trial identified in the retrieved literature has used an ACACB alteration as an eligibility biomarker or as a predictive marker of response. ACACB does not appear on any NCCN biomarker/targeted-therapy table — those tables list germline BRCA1/2 and PALB2, NTRK1/2/3 fusions, MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-H, RET fusions, BRAF V600E, HER2, FGFR2, IDH1, KRAS G12C, and NRG1 fusions, with no entry for ACACB or ACACA.[[1]][[2]][[3]] It is likewise absent from the tissue-agnostic FDA approvals (NTRK fusion, RET fusion, BRAF V600E, MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-H) and from the ESMO Precision Medicine Working Group's 2024 NGS recommendations.[[4]][[5]][[6]][[7]] No ACACB companion diagnostic exists.
ESCAT framing
ESCAT grades a specific alteration–drug–tumor context rather than a gene in the abstract.[[8]] Applied to any ACACB alteration with a proposed ACC inhibitor in any histology, the available data correspond to tier X — lack of evidence for actionability. The alteration does not reach tier IV either: tier IV requires preclinical evidence that the specific alteration predicts response to a matched agent, whereas the entire preclinical ACC literature tests pharmacologic enzyme inhibition in genotype-unselected models.[[8]]
The central conceptual distinction
ACC is a metabolic drug target, not a genomic biomarker, and the two are easily conflated when ACACB appears on an NGS report. In multiple myeloma models, sensitivity to the ACC inhibitors ND-646 and ND-630 did not correlate with ACC1 mRNA or protein expression, nor with immunoglobulin translocations or mutations.[[9]] Furthermore, the isoform repeatedly nominated as the cancer target is ACC1 (ACACA), not ACC2 (ACACB): ACC1 is the cytoplasmic isoform driving de novo lipogenesis, while ACC2 is tethered to the mitochondrial outer membrane, where local malonyl-CoA production restrains CPT1 and fatty acid oxidation.[[10]] ACACA, not ACACB, had the broadest cancer-dominant expression pattern in a systematic screen of metabolic isozyme targets.[[11]]
Alteration class matters as well. A truncating or deleted ACACB allele makes pharmacologic ACC2 inhibition mechanistically implausible as a therapeutic strategy; amplification does not establish increased enzyme activity or dependency; and missense variants in a gene encoding a ~2,450-residue protein accumulate readily as passengers on large panels, particularly in hypermutated tumors. No validated activating ACACB alteration class predicting ACC-inhibitor sensitivity has been described.
Clinical trial landscape for ACC inhibition
[[9]][[10]][[11]][[12]][[13]][[14]][[15]][[16]][[17]]
A 2026 review states explicitly that ND-646 and ND-654 have not progressed to clinical trials.[[18]] The firsocostat breast cancer IC50 of 80–93 µM is far above clinically achievable exposures and should be read as proof-of-concept only.[[13]] By contrast, the FASN inhibitor denifanstat (TVB-2640) in the same pathway has reached phase 3 — relevant context for how far behind ACC-directed oncology development sits.[[18]]
Biological uncertainty cutting the other way
ACC inhibition is not uniformly antitumor. Reported context-dependent procancer effects include increased acetyl-CoA availability leading to SMAD2 acetylation and EMT in a breast cancer model, AMPK-dependent ACC inactivation reducing PUFA-containing lipid synthesis and promoting ferroptosis resistance, and — most directly relevant to ACC2 — PHD3 loss with consequent ACC2 inhibition promoting tumor growth in acute myeloid leukemia and obesity-linked colon cancer models.[[19]] These are preclinical, context-specific observations rather than a demonstrated clinical hazard, but they add meaningful uncertainty to the premise that ACC2 blockade is therapeutically desirable.
Practical handling of an ACACB finding on a report
- Treat it as non-actionable and do not let it alter management. Re-read the report for the genuinely actionable co-alterations and tissue-agnostic markers listed above; confirm MSI/dMMR and TMB were assessed, since an ACACB missense variant in a hypermutated or MSI-H tumor is most plausibly a passenger and the hypermutation itself is the actionable finding.[[1]][[4]]
- ASCO guidelines recommend that for tumors with actionable alterations lacking an approved biomarker-linked therapy, clinical trial participation be encouraged after weighing expected efficacy of standard-of-care options (strong recommendation). ACACB does not meet the threshold of an actionable alteration under that framework, so trial enrollment should be driven by another driver alteration or by histology,[[20]] not by ACACB. ASCO also notes that not all variants affecting gene function are therapeutically actionable, and that reports should state when a variant lacks known function in oncogenesis.
- Refer to a molecular tumor board if the report is being used to justify off-label or trial-based therapy.[[21]][[22]]
- If the variant arose on germline testing, ACACB is not an established cancer susceptibility gene; NCCN principles state that a VUS should not be used to alter medical management, with screening and risk reduction based on personal and family history. The only ACC-family germline cancer-susceptibility data retrieved concern ACACA haplotypes and breast cancer risk, which were explicitly judged unlikely to be a major cause of high-risk susceptibility.[[23]][[24]][[25]]

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends a biomarker-linked targeted therapy for ACACB (ACC2) alterations, and no clinical trial has established ACACB as a predictive biomarker for any targeted agent in cancer. ACACB is not a recognized actionable oncogenic driver. It encodes acetyl-CoA carboxylase 2 (ACC2), a mitochondrial-membrane isoform of acetyl-CoA carboxylase whose product, malonyl-CoA, suppresses fatty acid oxidation by inhibiting CPT1 — in contrast to the cytoplasmic isoform ACC1 (ACACA), which drives de novo lipogenesis.[[1]][[2]] Current evidence for ACACB in oncology is limited to preclinical and biomarker-association studies, with no entry on any guideline's list of targetable alterations.
Guideline framing for a non-actionable alteration. Because there is no approved ACACB-linked therapy, the applicable guidance is the general framework for handling genomic alterations that lack a proven therapy:
- ASCO addresses this scenario directly. ASCO guidelines (2022 Provisional Clinical Opinion on somatic genomic testing) state that for tumors with actionable alterations but no approved biomarker-linked targeted therapy, enrollment in a clinical trial is the preferred option (strong recommendation), and that off-label use of therapies approved for other diseases is not recommended when a trial is available or without evidence of meaningful efficacy. ACACB falls into this category of alterations without an approved pairing.[[3]]
- NCCN and ESMO do not list ACACB among actionable biomarkers. NCCN's lists of targeted-therapy biomarkers (e.g., the NSCLC biomarker principles) do not include ACACB or ACACA,[[4]][[5]] and ESMO's ESCAT actionability tiering has not assigned ACACB a tier for any approved therapy.[[6]]
Preclinical/translational evidence (not practice-guiding). The therapeutic interest in this pathway centers on pharmacologic ACC inhibition, which is generally non-isoform-selective (inhibiting both ACC1/ACACA and ACC2/ACACB) rather than ACACB-specific:
- Dual ACC1/ACC2 inhibitor PF-05175157 (Pfizer; IC50 27 nmol/L for ACC1, 33 nmol/L for ACC2) showed broad in vitro and xenograft anti-cancer activity and synergy with FDA-approved agents including tyrosine kinase inhibitors and chemotherapy; it has only been tested clinically in healthy volunteers and type 2 diabetes (NCT01819922, NCT01792635, NCT01396161), not in cancer patients.[[7]][[8]]
- ND-646 / ND-630 (firsocostat) and other allosteric ACC inhibitors suppress fatty acid synthesis and tumor growth in NSCLC, multiple myeloma, prostate, and pancreatic preclinical models. Firsocostat has advanced only in non-o[[9]][[10]][[11]]ncologic (NASH) trials.
- Most of these data implicate ACC1 (ACACA) as the dominant lipogenic driver, with ACC2/ACACB expression often low or undetectable in tumor cells (e.g., NSCLC lines).[[2]][[9]]
The figure below, from the Svensson et al. NSCLC study in Nature Medicine, illustrates this isoform asymmetry — high ACC1 and low/undetectable ACC2 expression across NSCLC cell lines, with ACC1 (not ACC2) being required for fatty acid synthesis and tumor growth:
[[9]]
ACACB as a candidate biomarker (association only). In metastatic colorectal cancer, a bioinformatics-plus-validation study identified ACACB as a metabolism-related gene associated with cetuximab resistance, proposing it as a potential predictive biomarker via effects on EGFR phosphorylation and mTOR/Akt signaling.[[12]] This is hypothesis-generating and has not been validated prospectively or incorporated into any guideline.
Given the lack of any approved ACACB-targeted agent, the guideline-concordant pathway for a patient whose tumor harbors an ACACB alteration would be clinical trial enrollment per the ASCO framework.[[3]]

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends any AIRE-directed targeted therapy, and no interventional trial selecting patients by an AIRE alteration was identified in the retrieved literature. AIRE (autoimmune regulator, 21q22.3) is a transcriptional regulator of promiscuous tissue-restricted antigen expression in medullary thymic epithelial cells — not a kinase, not a druggable oncogenic driver, and not a validated predictive biomarker.[[1]][[2]] An AIRE variant on a somatic NGS report should not direct therapy selection or trial matching.
Guideline status is uniformly negative
- NCCN tumor-agnostic biomarker tables list only HER2 IHC 3+, NTRK1/2/3 fusion, RET fusion, MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-H (≥10 mut/Mb), and BRAF V600E — for example Colon Cancer COL-D-7 and Breast Cancer BINV-Q-7. AIRE appears in none of these.[[3]][[4]]
- The ESMO Precision Medicine Working Group 2024 NGS recommendations do not include AIRE among alterations to report or act on.[[5]]
- The JSCO–ESMO–ASCO–JSMO–TOS international consensus on tumour-agnostic treatment covers only MSI/dMMR and NTRK fusions, with ALK, BRAF, BRCAness, FGFR, HER2/HER3, HRD, KRAS, RET, ROS1, and TMB-high named as the alterations under active investigation.[[6]]
- Under the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (ESCAT), no tier has been assigned to AIRE by ESMO. Applying the framework's definitions, the available data (mouse models only) would correspond to tier IV at best and tier X — lack of evidence for actionability — in most contexts; this is an interpretation, not a published ESMO classification.[[7]]
What the evidence actually consists of
All AIRE-directed therapeutic work is preclinical and concerns modulating AIRE expression, not treating an AIRE sequence alteration:
- Engineered alteration of AIRE expression in tumor cells reset their "immunological selfness," converted a tolerized T-cell compartment into a tumor-reactive one, and conferred de novo checkpoint-blockade sensitivity on immunologically cold murine tumors; patient RNA-seq showed AIRE expression correlated with markers of TCR signaling and predicted response to immunotherapy. This is hypothesis-generating and has not entered clinical testing.[[8]]
- Transient RANKL blockade selectively depleted AIRE-expressing mTECs, produced an acquired defect in negative selection, and enhanced anti-tumor responses in the B16 melanoma model. Although a RANKL antibody is clinically available, this strategy has not been tested as an immunotherapy-sensitizing approach, and deliberate disruption of central tolerance carries an obvious autoimmunity risk.[[9]]
AIRE expression is prognostic, not predictive, and the direction is tumor- and compartment-dependent
[[10]][[11]][[12]][[13]][[14]]
None of these is used for treatment selection in any guideline.
The two AIRE contexts that do change management — neither involves targeted therapy
- Germline biallelic loss-of-function AIRE (APECED/APS-1). Chronic oral and esophageal candidiasis leads to oral or esophageal squamous cell carcinoma in roughly 5% of adults with long-standing mucosal candidiasis. In the Norwegian long-term cohort, neoplasms occurred in 10 of 49 class[[15]]ical APS-1 patients, and cancer accounted for 27% of deaths; all three patients with esophageal cancer died (mean age 48). Expert management recommends routine oral examination in partnership with dental colleagues and routine gastrointestinal cancer screening for all patients, with gastric mapping for intestinal metaplasia or dysplasia; no society guideline specifies a surveillance interval. Smoking and poorly controlled cand[[16]]idiasis are the recognized co-factors in reported oral tongue cancer cases, though it is unproven that aggressive antifungal therapy prevents carcinoma. Multidisciplinary care at a tertiary center and genetics referral are the appropriate framework. If an "AIRE mutation" is reported at germ[[17]]line-range allele fraction or with a compatible phenotype, pursue confirmatory germline testing rather than dismissing it as a passenger — lack of therapeutic actionability is not the same as lack of clinical significance.
- Thymic epithelial tumors. Approximately 95% of thymomas fail to express AIRE, which underlies paraneoplastic autoimmunity (myasthenia gravis, pure red cell aplasia, [Good syndrome](/rare-disease/good-syndrome)). This is loss of expression in the[[18]][[19]][[20]] tumor, not a targetable genomic lesion, and it has not been validated as a patient-level predictor of toxicity. The actionable guideline statement is histology-based: NCCN states that PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor therapy is not recommended for patients with thymoma, and that in thymic carcinoma there is concern for a higher rate of immune-related adverse events such as myocarditis than in most other malignancies; PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors are also not recommended in the neoadjuvant setting. Pembrolizumab is a preferred subsequent-line option in thymic carcinoma only. A meta-analysis of six trials (n=166) found grade 3–5 irAEs in 58.3% of thymoma versus 17.1% of thymic carcinoma patients; a single-center series reported irAEs in all thymoma patients tre[[21]][[22]]ated with ICIs. Accurate histologic separation of thymoma from thymic carcinoma (CD5, c-KIT, GLUT-1) is therefore a safety step.[[23]][[24]]
Terminology caution
"AIRE" is ambiguous in the oncology literature: some papers use it as an abbreviation for adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing, an entirely separate ADAR1-mediated post-transcriptional process — for example an AIRE-based immune subtyping scheme in bladder cancer.[[14]] If the question concerns A-to-I RNA editing rather than the autoimmune regulator gene, the relevant therapeutic landscape is ADAR1-directed, and clarification of which is meant would change the answer.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommends any targeted therapy selected by AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene status, and no clinical trial has validated AIRE as a predictive biomarker for a specific drug. AIRE is not an actionable oncologic driver alteration. It does not appear among the ~50 driver alterations and 74 genome-targeted drugs recommended across NCCN guidelines that were catalogued and scored for clinical actionability using the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of Molecular Targets (ESCAT) and ESMO-Magnitude of Clinical Benefit Scale.[[1]] In other words, AIRE carries no ESCAT tier and has no companion-diagnostic or guideline-endorsed matched therapy.
Why AIRE is biologically interesting but not a therapeutic target. AIRE is a transcription factor that enforces central immune tolerance by driving promiscuous tissue-specific self-antigen expression in medullary thymic epithelial cells, enabling negative selection of autoreactive T cells; biallelic loss causes APECED/APS-1 (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy).[[2]][[3]][[4]] Its relevance to cancer is almost entirely at the level of antitumor immunity and prognosis rather than as a mutated, druggable oncogene:
- Immune tolerance to tumor antigens. Because many AIRE-regulated self-antigens are shared cancer antigens (e.g., melanoma antigens such as TRP-1/TYRP1, and MAGE/GAGE cancer-testis antigens), AIRE-driven negative selection blunts antitumor T-cell responses. AIRE-deficient mice show rescued antigen-specific T cells and enhanced melanoma rejection, and AIRE polymorphisms that lower expression have been associated with melanoma protection.[[3]][[5]][[6]]
- Prognostic, not predictive, associations. Extrathymic/tumor AIRE expression has variable prognostic significance by tumor type — associated with better relapse-free survival in breast cancer (especially ER-positive), but with worse outcomes in osteosarcoma, oral squamous cell carcinoma, and in breast cancer tumor-associated neutrophils/macrophages. None of these associations have been translated into a treatment-selection rule.[[7]][[8]][[9]][[10]]
Experimental / preclinical approaches (hypothesis-generating only). Several strategies manipulate AIRE to enhance antitumor immunity, but all remain preclinical with no human trial evidence:
- Transient RANKL blockade to deplete AIRE-expressing mTECs enhanced antitumor responses in a B16 melanoma model.[[3]]
- Engineered modulation of AIRE expression within tumor cells ("resetting immunological selfness") converted immunologically cold tumors into targets for T-cell attack and conferred de novo sensitivity to checkpoint blockade in mouse models; in that work, tumor AIRE expression also correlated with response to immune therapies in patient RNA-seq data — a correlative signal, not a validated predictive biomarker.[[11]]
- AIRE-based immune subtyping has been proposed for bladder cancer immunotherapy stratification, but this is a computational/translational framework, not a guideline-endorsed test. (Note the bladder-cancer paper uses "AIRE" to denote adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing, a different entity from the AIRE gene — a[[12]] genuine acronym collision worth flagging.)
Practical implication. If an AIRE alteration or AIRE expression result is reported on a tumor molecular profile, there is currently no on- or off-label targeted agent, and no guideline or trial directs therapy on that basis. Treatment should continue to follow the validated, tumor-specific actionable alterations in the relevant NCCN/ASCO/ESMO guideline.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO recommendation and no clinical trial evidence supports targeted therapy directed at ANKRD13A alterations. ANKRD13A (ankyrin repeat domain containing 13A) is a genuine human gene, but it is not an actionable oncology biomarker: no identified guideline lists it, no therapy targets it, and no biomarker-selected trial enrolls on the basis of it. It does not appear in the NCCN biomarker-testing tables for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCL-19, NSCL-H), breast cancer (BINV-Q-7), colon cancer (COL-D-7), or gastric/esophagogastric cancer (GAST-B, ESOPH-B), and it is not among the FDA tumor-agnostic biomarkers — MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-H ≥10 mut/Mb, NTRK1/2/3 fusion, BRAF V600E, RET fusion, and HER2 IHC 3+.[[1]][[2]][[3]][[4]][[5]][[6]][[7]][[8]][[9]]
What is actually known about ANKRD13A
All existing data are preclinical and mechanistic, with no therapeutic translation:
- Ubiquitin-binding adaptor. The protein has N-terminal ankyrin repeats and four C-terminal ubiquitin-interacting motifs (UIMs) that recognize K63-linked polyubiquitin chains.[[10]][[11]]
- EGFR trafficking. ANKRD13A scaffolds a transient complex with activated EGFR and the E3 ligases ITCH and RNF11, promoting lysosomal sorting of the receptor. This is the only connection to a druggable pathway, and it is indirect.[[11]]
- Cell-death checkpoint. It binds ubiquitinated RIP1 within TNF signaling complex-II and raises the threshold for TNF-induced death; higher expression correlated inversely with apoptosis and with poorer prognosis in ovarian cancer tissue.[[12]]
- Mitophagy and other roles. It recruits VCP to depolarized mitochondria during PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and participates in CYYR1-mediated degradation of the E3 ligase WWP1.[[10]][[13]]
Likely confusions with other ANKRD-family genes
If the finding came off a sequencing report, verify the exact gene symbol, since neighboring family members carry different implications:
[[10]][[11]][[12]][[13]][[14]][[15]][[16]][[17]]
How to handle this on a genomic report
The one scenario in which an "ANKRD13A alteration" could be actionable is a structural rearrangement in which ANKRD13A is the 5' partner of a druggable kinase — in that case the retained kinase domain (e.g., RET, NTRK, ALK, ROS1, BRAF) governs treatment, and the breakpoint structure and fusion-partner annotation should be confirmed on the report before any decision. NCCN cautions that nonspecific terminology such as "rearrangement" without the specific fusion structure or genomic breakpoints should be avoided on reports.[[18]]
Absent such a fusion, an ANKRD13A single-nucleotide variant or copy-number change falls into AMP/ASCO/CAP tier III, variant of unknown clinical significance — variants lacking convincing evidence of cancer association.[[19]] NCCN states plainly that variants of uncertain significance should not be used to alter medical management.[[20]][[21]] Therapy should be directed by the validated alterations on the same report; if none are present, ASCO guidelines recommend multigene genomic testing to determine candidacy for tumor-agnostic therapies, and off-label genomic biomarker–linked treatment should be delivered within a clinical trial whenever possible, since an alteration predictive of response in one tumor type may not be predictive in another.[[18]]
Two caveats on the tumor-agnostic options themselves: the dabrafenib/trametinib BRAF V600E solid-tumor approval excludes colorectal cancer, and selpercatinib — not pralsetinib — carries the tumor-agnostic RET fusion indication; pralsetinib's approvals remain restricted to NSCLC and thyroid cancer.[[7]][[22]]
This conclusion reflects the literature retrieved as of October 2026; it remains possible that an ANKRD13A-selected cohort exists within a broad basket protocol, but enrollment permissiveness is not the same as evidence that the alteration predicts benefit.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommends any targeted therapy for CRACD alterations, and no clinical trial evidence currently addresses CRACD as a therapeutic target or biomarker in cancer. CRACD (Capping protein inhibiting Regulator of Actin Dynamics; also called CRAD/KIAA1211) is a tumor suppressor that promotes actin polymerization by inhibiting the capping proteins CAPZA and CAPZB.[[1]] It is not a recognized actionable driver alteration in any current guideline. For context, the ASCO Living Guideline on stage IV NSCLC with driver alterations addresses only ALK, ROS1, BRAF V600E, MET exon 14 skipping, RET, and NTRK (plus EGFR/KRAS G12C in companion documents) — CRACD is not among the recognized targetable alterations.[[2]][[3]] All available CRACD evidence is preclinical.
What the preclinical evidence actually shows. CRACD is recurrently inactivated across several tumor types, and the therapeutic interest is in exploiting the downstream vulnerabilities created by its loss rather than restoring or inhibiting CRACD itself:
- Gastric cancer. CRACD is frequently inactivated in gastric cancer, with enrichment in the mucinous subtype. In genetically engineered organoid and syngeneic/orthotopic mouse models, Cracd loss (combined with Kras mutation and Trp53 loss) drove mucinous plasticity and immune escape via actin dysregulation → NF-κB/COX2 and NADPH oxidase–dependent ROS → HIF1α stabilization → PD-L1 transactivation. Pharmacologic HIF1α inhibition (PX-478) or PD-L1 blockade restored immune surveillance and suppressed tumor growth, identifying the HIF1α–PD-L1 axis as a candidate therapeutic vulnerability in CRACD-low gastric cancer. This is entirely preclinical, and the authors explicitly call for validation in patient cohorts and incorporation of CRACD testing into immunotherapy trials before clinical use.[[1]]
- [Small cell lung cancer](/rare-disease/small-cell-lung-cancer). CRACD is mutated in roughly 11–16% of SCLC tumors/cell lines. Preclinical models show Cracd loss drives neuroendocrine plasticity (via NOTCH downregulation and ASCL1 de-repression) and immune evasion through EZH2-mediated MHC-I suppression, suggesting these pathways as potential vulnerabilities — again without any clinical trial or guideline endorsement.[[4]]
- Colorectal cancer / lung adenocarcinoma. CRACD loss destabilizes the cadherin-catenin-actin complex, releasing β-catenin and hyperactivating WNT signaling (linked to intestinal mucinous adenomas), and is associated with neuroendocrine plasticity in lung adenocarcinoma.[[1]]
The following figure summarizes the proposed CRACD-loss → ROS–HIF1α–PD-L1 signaling cascade from the gastric cancer study that underlies the hypothesized therapeutic strategy:
[[1]]
Important disambiguation. "CRAC" and "CRACD" are easily confused with unrelated targets. Calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channel inhibition (e.g., RP4010) has preclinical anti-tumor data in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma — but this concerns an ion channel, not the CRACD actin-regulatory tumor suppressor.[[5]] Similarly, CRAF/RAF1 is a distinct kinase in the MAPK pathway.[[6]] None of these has guideline-endorsed targeted therapy tied specifically to the "CRACD" gene.
The practical takeaway: if a CRACD alteration is identified on a tumor sequencing panel, there is currently no guideline-directed targeted therapy and no approved or trial-validated matched treatment. Management should follow standard histology- and stage-specific guidelines for the underlying cancer.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends any therapy selected on the basis of CRACD status, and no clinical trial — interventional or reported CRACD-defined cohort — was identified in the retrieved literature. CRACD (capping protein inhibiting regulator of actin dynamics; also reported as CRAD or KIAA1211) appears in the cancer literature exclusively as a preclinical tumor suppressor, characterized in mouse models, organoids, and TCGA analyses of [small cell lung cancer](/rare-disease/small-cell-lung-cancer), gastric cancer, and colorectal cancer[[1]].[[2]] It is not a biomarker with any established therapeutic actionability.
What the guidelines actually say about the relevant disease settings
- NCCN Small Cell Lung Cancer (Version 1.2027/2026) lists only "consider biomarker testing," restricted to rare circumstances — extensive-stage/relapsed disease in patients who do not smoke, lightly smoke, have remote smoking history, or present a diagnostic or therapeutic dilemma — and names no specific gene targets at all.[[3]]
- ASCO guidelines state in Recommendation 7.1 of the Systemic Therapy for SCLC rapid update that there is no evidence supporting molecular profiling or biomarker analysis to guide standard treatment in de novo SCLC (evidence strength: weak; recommendation strength: weak), and that to date no predictive biomarker has a validated role in guiding SCLC treatment.[[4]]
- NCCN Gastric Cancer (Version 2026) biomarker testing is limited to HER2/ERBB2, PD-L1, MMR/MSI, CLDN18.2, BRAF V600E, NTRK1/2/3, and RET. CRACD is absent.[[5]]
- ASCO guidelines recommend testing for PD-L1, dMMR/MSI-H, CLDN18.2, and HER2 in gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma, with broad NGS considered for pan-tumor biomarkers — CRACD is not among them.[[6]]
- ESMO: the ESMO Precision Medicine Working Group NGS recommendations do not include CRACD among tested or actionable targets. Under the ESMO Scale for[[7]] Clinical Actionability of Molecular Targets, a target supported only by preclinical data falls in tier IV (preclinical evidence of actionability), not tiers I–III. No ESMO SCLC- or gastric-specific guideline text addressing CRACD was retrieved.[[8]]
The preclinical basis, and why it has not reached the clinic
Two mechanistic hypotheses generate the "targeted therapy" framing, both from genetically engineered mouse and organoid work:
- SCLC — EZH2 inhibition. CRACD is mutated in 11–16% of SCLC tumors and cell lines and is transcriptionally downregulated relative to normal lung. Cracd knockout drives neuroendocrine plasticity via NOTCH downregulation and de-repression of ASCL1, and produces EZH2-mediated epigenetic silencing of MHC-I with T-cell exclusion; the authors propose EZH2 blockade[[1]] as a strategy for CRACD-inactivated SCLC and explicitly note that EZH2 monotherapy may not suffice and that combination with checkpoint blockade requires study.
- Gastric cancer — HIF1α/PD-L1 axis. CRACD loss activates NF-κB/COX2 and NOX1-dependent ROS, stabilizing HIF1α and transactivating PD-L1; the HIF1α inhibitor PX-478 or anti-PD-L1 suppressed tumor growth and metastasis in murine models. The investigators state directly that CRACD should not replace PD-L1 CPS, MSI, or EBV status, that it is at best a complementary candidate biomarker, and that validation in larger annotated cohorts treated with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade is required before any clinical implementation.[[2]]
The EZH2/EZH1 trials in SCLC exist but are not CRACD-selected
None of these trials stratified by, enrolled on, or reported a CRACD-defined subgroup, so they do not constitute evidence for CRACD-directed therapy.
[[9]][[10]][[11]]
Separately, the FDA has alerted clinicians to an increased risk of new blood cancers with tazemetostat, and the sponsor is voluntarily withdrawing the product from the US market — relevant if off-label EZH2 inhibition is being contemplated.[[12]]
Practical interpretation of a CRACD alteration on an NGS report
A reported CRACD alteration should not change management. Treat according to the standard histology- and stage-based algorithm and the established biomarkers for that tumor type. Two qualifications are worth preserving: the preclinical hypotheses concern functional CRACD inactivation (biallelic/truncating loss or demonstrated protein downregulation by IHC), and cannot be extrapolated to an arbitrary missense variant, monoallelic loss, or a histology outside those studied.[[1]][[2]] Lack of therapeutic actionability also does not by itself make a variant a VUS — pathogenicity classification and actionability classification are separate determinations, and the report's own annotation governs the former. Off-label EZH2 or HIF1α inhibition on the basis of CRACD status is not supported outside a clinical trial.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommendation, no FDA-approved agent, and no biomarker-selected clinical trial addressing targeted therapy for DENND2C alterations was identified in the retrieved literature. DENND2C does not appear in any NCCN biomarker-directed therapy table (e.g., NSCLC NSCL-J, breast BINV-Q-7, biliary BIL-C-3, neuroendocrine NE-G-7), is not among the genes for which ESMO's Precision Medicine Working Group recommends tumor NGS-directed therapy, and is not listed among the therapeutically actionable alterations in the ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion on somatic genomic testing.[[1]][[2]][[3]][[4]][[5]][[6]] There is no published trial cohort, matched agent, or efficacy signal selected on DENND2C status.
What the gene is
DENND2C encodes a DENN-domain protein. The DENN domain family comprises Rab-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factors; family-wide characterization placed the DENND2 proteins as GEFs controlling Rab9-dependent trafficking of mannose-6-phosphate receptor to lysosomes, with localization to actin filaments.[[7]][[8]][[9]] Structural and cell-based work has extended the substrate repertoire of several DENN proteins, but these studies are family- or paralog-level and do not establish a driver function for DENND2C specifically.[[10]][[11]] No oncogenic driver role, recurrent hotspot, recurrent fusion, or hereditary cancer syndrome association for DENND2C emerged from the search.
How to classify the finding
- AMP/ASCO/CAP (somatic framework): a variant in a gene not convincingly associated with cancer falls into tier III — variants of unknown clinical significance, which explicitly includes variants in genes not previously reported in any cancer. This, rather than the germ[[12]]line VUS framework, is the appropriate lens for a tumor NGS finding.
- ESCAT: the scale assigns a tier to a specific alteration–drug–tumor-type triplet, not to a gene. An alteration with no preclinical or clinical evidence of actionability corresponds to tier X (lack of evidence for actionability).[[13]][[14]]
- ASCO's PCO stresses that most alterations detected by sequencing are passengers, that clinical decisions must incorporate the known or predicted functional impact of the specific alteration plus clinical efficacy data for targeting it, and that functional annotation on the report should be read rather than the gene list alone.[[6]]
Do not extrapolate from paralogs
Most cancer literature in this family concerns different genes, and none of it supports treating DENND2C:
[[7]][[8]][[10]][[15]][[16]][[17]][[18]][[19]]
Because DENND2B and DENND2D are frequently discussed in oncology contexts, confirming the exact gene symbol, transcript, and alteration type (missense vs truncating vs copy number) on the report is worthwhile. A copy-number call at this locus may also represent a bystander within a larger segmental chromosome 1p event rather than a discrete gene-level lesion.
Practical approach
1. Re-review the report for alterations that are actionable, including tumor-agnostic biomarkers — MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-H (≥10 mut/Mb), NTRK1/2/3 fusion, RET fusion, BRAF V600E, HER2 IHC 3+ — recognizing that each carries its own tumor-type, prior-therapy, and assay restrictions and that several are accelerated approvals limited to patients with no satisfactory alternatives.[[1]][[2]][[3]][[4]]
2. Consider molecular tumor board review, where ESCAT I/II assignment has been associated with higher response rates and better PFS/OS among patients receiving matched therapy.[[20]]
3. Clinical trial referral is the recommended route for alterations without an approved matched therapy, after weighing the expected efficacy of available standard-of-care options (ASCO PCO 4.2, strong recommendation). Enrollment in a basket trial would, in practice, hinge on a co-occurring alteration rather than on DENND2C.[[6]]
4. Set expectations accordingly: in a national registry of >54,000 patients undergoing comprehensive genomic profiling, 72.7% had a potentially actionable alteration but only ~8% received matched targeted therapy.[[21]][[22]]
The negative finding here is a statement about the retrieved literature as of this search; it means no DENND2C-selected treatment cohort or guideline recommendation was identified, not that any society has issued an explicit recommendation against targeting the gene.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommendation and no clinical trial identifies DENND2C as an actionable target, and no targeted therapy exists for DENND2C alterations. A search of the medical literature returned no guideline statement, no biomarker-matched trial, and no FDA-approved agent directed at DENND2C (DENN domain-containing 2C). DENND2C is not listed among the therapeutically actionable biomarkers in precision-oncology frameworks, and it does not appear in catalogs of validated cancer driver genes derived from large pan-cancer sequencing efforts.[[1]][[2]][[3]]
What is known about the gene family is limited and not therapeutically actionable:
- The DENND2 family encodes guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that regulate Rab GTPases involved in membrane trafficking. The best-studied member in oncology is DENND2D (not DENND2C), which behaves as a candidate tumor suppressor silenced by promoter hypermethylation in hepatocellular, esophageal, gastric, and non-small cell lung cancers, where downregulation predicts worse prognosis. These are prognostic/biomarker observations, not targets with a matched drug.[[4]][[5]]
- The related gene DENN/MADD has been studied preclinically as an anti-apoptotic factor whose antisense knockdown induces apoptosis and tumor regression in models, but this has not advanced to any targeted clinical agent.[[6]][[7]]
- No published data specifically characterize DENND2C as a driver or establish any drug-variant match for it.
How such an alteration should be handled clinically. The ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion on somatic genomic testing is the relevant framework: clinical decisions should incorporate (1) the known or predicted functional impact of the alteration on protein function and (2) clinical efficacy data for targeting it with a specific agent.[[1]] For DENND2C, neither exists—most sequenced alterations are passengers rather than actionable drivers, and an alteration in a gene with no functional annotation and no drug-sensitivity data should not be treated as targetable.[[1]]
Practical pathway if a DENND2C alteration is reported. Because no on-label or guideline-endorsed targeted option applies, the appropriate route is review by a molecular tumor board and consideration of a genomically-matched basket trial (e.g., TAPUR, DRUP, or the Danish ProTarget trial), which match EMA/FDA-approved targeted drugs to actionable alterations outside their labeled indications—though eligibility in these platforms still requires an alteration with an established drug-variant match, which DENND2C currently lacks.[[8]]

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommendation and no clinical trial addresses targeted therapy for FAM117A alterations. FAM117A is not a biomarker in any FDA-approved oncology label, is not among the actionable genes curated by OncoKB (~161 genes as of 2023), and does not appear in the actionable-mutation-of-interest lists used to assign therapy in the major genomically driven basket platforms — NCI-MATCH (EAY131, NCT02465060), ComboMATCH, Pediatric MATCH (NCT03155620), or ASCO's TAPUR (NCT02693535).[[1]][[2]][[3]][[4]] On the ESMO ESCAT framework, which ranks biomarker–drug pairs by evidence level, a FAM117A alteration has no published biomarker–drug pair and would therefore sit at tier X (lack of evidence for actionability) — an inference from the framework's definitions, not a formal ESMO assignment, since ESCAT tiering is alteration- and tumor-type-specific and is assigned per biomarker–drug pair.[[5]]
What evidence does exist is preclinical and expression-based, not mutation-based
- Lung adenocarcinoma / CDK4/6 signal: A TCGA bioinformatics study with cell-line and xenograft follow-up found that low FAM117A expression was the strongest survival-related factor for poor outcome; FAM117A overexpression suppressed G1→S transition, knockdown promoted proliferation, and tumor growth driven by FAM117A depletion was blocked by palbociclib (PD0332991). This is hypothesis-generating only. The predictor was mRNA expression, not a genomic alteration, and no clinical study has tested a CDK4/6 inhibitor selected on FAM117A status.[[6]]
- Gastric carcinogenesis: Integrated ATAC-seq and whole-transcriptome profiling across normal mucosa, precancerous lesions, and gastric cancer identified FAM117A (with PIGU) as a regulatory factor modulating p53 signaling and E-/N-cadherin, proposed as a biomarker and potential therapeutic target. Again entirely preclinical, with no drug–biomarker pair.[[7]]
FAM117A itself encodes a CRTC-interacting/ALS2CR13-family protein with no described druggable catalytic pocket; no kinase, no enzymatic activity, and no synthetic-lethal partner has been validated.
How to handle a FAM117A alteration on a tumor NGS report
- Classify it as having no established therapy-predictive significance. This is distinct from calling it a variant of uncertain significance: a somatic alteration can be functionally real yet carry no predictive utility, and conversely a sequence variant may be uninterpretable. The ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion on somatic genomic testing makes exactly this point — not all variants that affect gene function are therapeutically actionable, and reports should flag variants of unknown significance explicitly.[[8]]
- Do not extrapolate the palbociclib preclinical data to off-label CDK4/6 inhibition. The signal was generated from expression manipulation in cell lines, and no matching trial cohort exists.
- Re-review the report for genuinely actionable findings, applying the tumor-type- and setting-specific restrictions on each rather than treating them as a generic checklist: MSI-H/dMMR and TMB-high (pembrolizumab, which in the TMB-H indication requires prior progression with no satisfactory alternatives and excludes pediatric CNS tumors), NTRK fusions without a known acquired resistance mutation (larotrectin[[9]]ib), and tumor-type-specific drivers. BRAF V600E, HER2, RET, and BRCA1/2-directed therapies carry histology-, line-, and assay-specific qualifiers and should be checked against the relevant disease guideline rather than applied tumor-agnostically.
- If FAM117A appears as a fusion partner, actionability depends on the full structure of the fusion — frame, retained functional domains, orientation, recurrence, and assay validation — not on the partner gene's identity alone, since the 5′ partner contributes promoter activity and dimerization domains. Most fusions detected by deep sequencing are non-recurrent passengers with no tumorigenic effect.[[10]]
- Molecular tumor board review and trial matching is the appropriate route if standard options are exhausted. MTB-directed matching improves outcomes for ESCAT tier II–III alterations, but FAM117A does not reach even tier III, so enrollment should be driven by other alterations, histology, or a phase I slot rather than by FAM117A itself.[[11]]
- FAM117A is not a cancer susceptibility gene; its presence on a tumor report is not an indication for germline referral. Referral should be driven by a co-occurring pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant in an established susceptibility gene or by personal/family history.[[12]][[13]]
One caveat on nomenclature: confirm the report refers to FAM117A rather than the paralog FAM117B, and check the transcript and HGVS designation, since the clinical interpretation of a report entry depends on which transcript the laboratory used.[[8]]

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommends any targeted therapy for FAM117A alterations, and no clinical trial has tested a FAM117A-directed or FAM117A-selected targeted therapy. FAM117A (family with sequence similarity 117 member A) does not appear on any established actionability framework — it is absent from the OncoKB levels of evidence, the AMP/ASCO/CAP tiers, and the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of Molecular Targets (ESCAT) used to rank druggable alterations.[[1]][[2]] The existing literature on FAM117A in cancer is limited to preclinical and bioinformatic studies describing it as a candidate prognostic biomarker, not a validated therapeutic target.
What the available evidence does show (preclinical/prognostic only):
- Lung adenocarcinoma: A 2022 TCGA-based bioinformatics and in vitro/xenograft study identified reduced FAM117A expression as associated with poor survival and found that FAM117A depletion promoted G1→S cell-cycle progression, with FAM117A-driven growth blocked by the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib (PD0332991) in cell lines and xenografts. This is hypothesis-generating preclinical work in which FAM117A expression level (not a mutation or fusion) was correlated with palbociclib sensitivity; it has not been transl[[3]]ated into any biomarker-selected trial.
- Gastric cancer: A 2025 whole-transcriptome/ATAC-seq study proposed FAM117A (with PIGU) as a regulator of p53 signaling and cell-adhesion molecules during gastric carcinogenesis, labeling it a "potential therapeutic target" on mechanistic grounds only, without any drug-targeting data.[[4]]
Why FAM117A is not currently actionable: The ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion on somatic genomic testing emphasizes that most detected alterations are passengers, that clinical decision-making requires both a known functional impact and clinical efficacy data for targeting the alteration with a specific agent, and that off-label use of genomic biomarker-linked therapy is not recommended without clinical evidence of meaningful efficacy.[[1]] FAM117A meets none of these thresholds — there is no agent approved or in trials selected by FAM117A status.
Practical implication: If a tumor harbors a FAM117A alteration alongside no established actionable driver, the appropriate pathway per ASCO is enrollment in a biomarker-agnostic or genomically-driven basket/platform trial (e.g., ProTarget [NCT04341181], TAPUR, DRUP), rather than off-label targeted therapy.[[1]][[5]] Note that none of these trials currently includes a FAM117A-defined cohort. The preclinical palbociclib signal in lung adenocarcinoma is insufficient to justify CDK4/6 inhibitor use outside of its approved HR+/HER2- breast cancer indications.[[3]][[6]]

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommends any targeted therapy for RFX7 alterations, and no clinical trial of an RFX7-directed therapy was identified in the retrieved literature. RFX7 is not among the actionable biomarkers listed in current oncology guidelines (which, for example, in advanced NSCLC cover EGFR, KRAS, BRAF, ERBB2/HER2, ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK, and MET exon 14, but not RFX7).[[1]][[2]] RFX7 remains an area of preclinical and translational research only; the available evidence is mechanistic (cell lines and mouse models) and prognostic, not therapeutic.
What the biology suggests (preclinical only). RFX7 is a winged-helix transcription factor that functions as a tumor suppressor, restraining cellular metabolism and MYC activity.[[3]][[4]][[5]] Its relevance to cancer is defined by loss-of-function, not a druggable gain-of-function target:
- B-cell lymphomas. RFX7 nonsense/frameshift mutations occur in roughly 3–5% of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and 13–15% of EBV-negative Burkitt lymphoma, and a polymorphism near the locus correlates with CLL prognosis in the unmutated subset. Truncated RFX7 causes both loss-of-function and dominant-negative effects, and low RFX7 mRNA correlates with worse DLBCL progression-free and overall survival. Because RFX7 loss de-represses MYC, the authors propose that RFX7-altered lymphomas may be candidates for MYC-targeted ag[[5]][[6]]ents currently in development—a hypothesis, not a validated or guideline-endorsed strategy.
- Glioblastoma. RFX7 is epigenetically silenced by promoter hypermethylation, disinhibiting the PIK3IP1–PI3K/AKT axis and promoting lactate-driven immunosuppression; in preclinical models, the lactate-production inhibitor stiripentol reduced tumor growth and improved response to immune checkpoint therapy. This is experimental rationale only.[[7]]
The clinical implication of RFX7 at present is prognostic/biomarker rather than predictive of response to any approved drug. The following figure from the 2026 Nature Immunology study maps the distribution of RFX7 mutations across lymphoid malignancies and the associated survival difference in DLBCL:
[[5]]
Given that RFX7-altered lymphomas are mechanistically linked to deregulated MYC, early-phase trials of MYC-pathway or related agents may be of interest for affected patients, though none specifically enroll by RFX7 status.

Because no RFX7-selective trial exists, the search above used the mechanistically linked MYC pathway in aggressive B-cell lymphoma as a proxy. The search returned 81 available trials; none enroll by RFX7 status. Among the top trials in the search results above, a few are mechanistically relevant to the RFX7–MYC axis: [NCT05755087](/clinical-trials/NCT05755087) (tegavivint, a β-catenin/TBL1 inhibitor that modulates MYC-associated Wnt signaling in R/R large B-cell lymphoma), [NCT06792734](/clinical-trials/NCT06792734) (BTM-3566, an agent in R/R mature B-cell lymphomas), and several targeted combinations such as [NCT06649812](/clinical-trials/NCT06649812) (ViPOR). These are included only as options potentially aligned with the underlying biology, not as RFX7-directed therapies.
The practical takeaway: RFX7 is currently a research-stage prognostic marker in lymphoid malignancies (and in GBM biology), without any guideline recommendation or dedicated clinical trial for RFX7-targeted treatment.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends any therapy selected on the basis of RFX7 alteration status, and no prospective trial that enrolled, stratified, or reported outcomes by RFX7 mutation was identified in the retrieved literature. RFX7 is not among the six biomarkers with tumor-agnostic FDA approvals (MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-H ≥10 mut/Mb, NTRK1/2/3 fusion, RET fusion, BRAF V600E, HER2 IHC 3+), and no RFX7-matched agent exists.[[1]][[2]][[3]][[4]] Everything supporting RFX7 as a therapeutic handle is preclinical — mouse models and cell lines.
What the guidelines actually contain
- NCCN B-Cell Lymphomas (v2026) — BCEL-A lists the minimal accepted gene set for a DLBCL multigene panel: ACTB, BCL2, BCL6, CARD11, CD79B, CREBBP, EZH2, KMT2D, MYC, MYD88, MEF2B, SOCS1, NOTCH2, BTK, PLCG2, TP53, ID3, TCF3, SMARCA4, CCND3, B2M, TNFRSF14, JAK/STAT, MAPK/ERK, NOTCH1, PDL1/PDL2, IL4R, ITPKB, NFKBIE, STAT6, XPO1, PIM1, ATM, BIRC3, NSD2, and UBR5. RFX7 is not on this list. Only EZH2 and SMARCB1 are annotated as having treatment significance (EZH2 inhibitors).[[5]]
- NCCN T-Cell Lymphomas (v2026) — the biomarker testing principles (TCLYM-A) cover TRB/TRG rearrangements, ALK, TET2/IDH2/RHOA/DNMT3A, and STAT3/STAT5B, with no mention of RFX7.[[6]]
- ESMO Precision Medicine Working Group — the 2020 and 2024 NGS recommendations do not include lymphoma among tumor types with a routine NGS indication, and name no RFX7-directed action.[[7]][[8]]
- ESCAT — ESMO has not assigned RFX7 a tier. The available data (cell lines, genetically engineered mice) correspond to the preclinical category of the scale, which explicitly does not support clinical use.[[9]][[10]]
Note that the searches performed here were centered on lymphoid malignancy and pan-cancer precision-oncology guidance, where RFX7 alterations are concentrated; absence of an RFX7 recommendation elsewhere is inferred from the tumor-agnostic approval landscape rather than from a page-by-page review of every disease-site guideline.
Why RFX7 appears on panels at all
RFX7 is a p53-pathway transcription factor and bona fide tumor suppressor. Loss-of-function nonsense and frameshift mutations occur in 3–5% of DLBCL and 13–15% of EBV-negative Burkitt lymphoma, and a polymorphism near the locus is associated with CLL, where mutations carry prognostic weight in the IGHV-unmutated subset.[[11]][[12]] Truncated RFX7 proteins are both loss-of-function and dominant-negative over wild-type RFX7, which explains the relevance of heterozygous mutations.[[11]] Low RFX7 transcript abundance independently correlates with worse DLBCL outcome, even without a coding mutation.[[11]][[12]] TP53 aberration co-occurs in 30–70% of RFX7-mutant BL/DLBCL cases.[[11]] So the signal is prognostic/biological, not predictive.
Preclinical therapeutic hypotheses (none clinically validated)
[[11]][[12]][[13]][[14]][[15]][[16]][[17]]
Practical implication
An RFX7 mutation reported on a lymphoma NGS panel is pathogenic but not clinically actionable — it should be interpreted as a biologic/prognostic finding rather than a treatment biomarker, and it should not prompt a change in therapy or a search for a matched agent. Treatment remains histology-, stage-, and fitness-directed per the applicable NCCN algorithm. The co-occurring alterations that do carry classification or risk implications in this setting are TP53 mutation and MYC with BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangement.[[5]][[18]] If an RFX7-mutant patient has exhausted standard options, the appropriate route is a molecularly unselected or broad basket early-phase trial, not an RFX7-matched one.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends a targeted therapy for "RP1 alterations," and no clinical trial evidence supports targeting an RP1 gene alteration as an actionable oncogenic driver. RP1 is not an established, therapeutically actionable driver gene in any solid or hematologic malignancy. Across the major precision-oncology frameworks referenced by ASCO—OncoKB, AMP/ASCO/CAP, ESCAT, and CIViC—RP1 does not appear as a gene with a biomarker-linked approved or guideline-endorsed therapy.[[1]] A large driver-gene discovery analysis of 10,478 cancer genomes likewise did not identify RP1 among actionable driver alterations; the recurrently actionable targets were genes such as PIK3CA, KRAS, and PTEN.[[2]]
An important caveat is that "RP1" is ambiguous, and the most likely intended meanings each lead to the same conclusion—no biomarker-directed therapy:
- RP1 ([retinitis pigmentosa](/rare-disease/retinitis-pigmentosa) 1 / "oxygen-regulated protein," an EB1-family APC- and tubulin-binding protein on chromosome 18q21). This locus lies in a region deleted in up to ~50% of colorectal cancers, and the protein participates in microtubule dynamics and the mitotic cytokinesis checkpoint, but no targeted agent exploits RP1 status. The germline cancer-predisposition literature, including a recent large UK Biobank analysis of 96[[3]] predisposition genes, does not list RP1 among genes conferring cancer risk or informing therapy.[[4]]
- Long noncoding RNAs with "RP1-" clone-based names (e.g., RP1-59D14.5 in prostate cancer, RP1-228H13.5 in liver cancer). These are preclinical/bioinformatic findings describing tumor-suppressor or oncogenic ceRNA roles; none is a validated clinical biomarker or drug target.[[5]][[6]]
- Ribosomal proteins (RPs) broadly. RPs are studied as prognostic/diagnostic biomarkers across colorectal, breast, and prostate cancers, but again without a biomarker-linked targeted therapy in any guideline.[[7]][[8]][[9]][[10]]
Separately, note that "RP1" is also a drug name—vusolimogene oderparvec, an investigational HSV-1–based oncolytic immunotherapy (studied in melanoma and other tumors). That is a therapeutic agent, not a tumor "alteration," so if the intended question concerns that product rather than a gene, the framing would be different; please clarify if so.
Where a genomic alteration lacks an approved biomarker-linked therapy, both ASCO and ESMO frameworks direct that clinical-trial enrollment is the preferred pathway, and ASCO explicitly recommends against off-label use of biomarker-linked drugs absent a clinical trial or evidence of meaningful efficacy.[[1]] In practical terms, an RP1 finding on a sequencing report should be interpreted through functional annotation and an actionability knowledge base before any treatment inference is drawn.[[1]]

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends targeted therapy for RP1 gene alterations, and no RP1 alteration–selected clinical trial was identified in the retrieved literature. The term is ambiguous, and the two plausible readings resolve differently.
"RP1" as a gene is not an actionable oncologic target
- RP1 ([retinitis pigmentosa](/rare-disease/retinitis-pigmentosa) 1) encodes a photoreceptor-specific, microtubule-associated ciliary protein containing a doublecortin domain, required for outer segment disc morphogenesis. Pathogenic variants cause autosomal dominant and recessive retinitis pigmentosa. It is not a cancer predisposition gene, and no targeted agent exists for RP1-altered tumors.[[1]][[2]]
- "RP1" is also a legacy name for MAPRE2/EB2, a member of the EB1 microtubule-binding family that interacts with APC. Evidence here is entirely preclinical: MAPRE2 overexpression associates with perineural invasion in pancreatic cancer and with worse survival and an immunosuppressed microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma, with knockdown suppressing proliferation and invasion in vitro. No clinical agent, trial, or guideline recommendation follows from this.[[3]][[4]][[5]][[6]]
- "RP1-" prefixed lncRNAs (e.g., RP1-59D14.5 in prostate cancer) are genomic clone-based names, not druggable targets.[[7]]
The governing framework is the ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion on somatic genomic testing, which states that clinical decisions should incorporate both the known functional impact of the alteration and clinical efficacy data for targeting it; most alterations detected by sequencing are passengers, and not all alterations in a gene confer drug sensitivity.[[8]] An RP1 variant on an NGS report meets neither criterion. Practically: confirm the gene/transcript given the naming overlap, determine somatic versus germline (a germline RP1 variant carries ophthalmologic and genetic-counseling implications, not oncologic ones), and base therapy on independently assessed actionable co-alterations, TMB, and MMR/MSI status.
"RP1" as a drug — vusolimogene oderparepvec — is guideline-recommended but not biomarker-directed
RP1 is the development code for vusolimogene oderparepvec, an oncolytic HSV-1 engineered to express GM-CSF and the fusogenic glycoprotein GALV-GP-R−.[[9]][[10]] Eligibility depends on injectable lesions and prior anti–PD-1 failure, not on any RP1 genotype — an RP1 sequence variant is not an indication for this agent.
[[9]][[11]][[12]][[13]][[14]][[15]]
Two caveats on the approval. The label reports ORR 24.2% and median DOR 14.1 months in the efficacy-evaluable population, lower than the published 32.9%/33.7 months; approval followed two complete response letters reflecting FDA concern about response durability and the adequacy of the efficacy-evaluable population.[[16]] Dosing per the IGNYTE protocol and label is intratumoral injection every 2 weeks for 8 doses, sized by lesion dimension to a maximum of 10 mL per dose, at 10⁶ PFU/mL for the first dose then 10⁷ PFU/mL thereafter, with nivolumab 240 mg IV q2w for 16 weeks then 480 mg q4w to 24 months — the product label's lesion-size dosing table should be followed rather than any simplified rule.[[9]] IGNYTE excluded patients with uncontrolled/untreated CNS metastases, active or prior hepatitis B/C or HIV, prior severe HSV-1 complications, chronic systemic corticosteroids, and prior oncolytic therapy.[[9]] As with other HSV-1–based oncolytic agents, herpetic risk makes immunocompromise and pregnancy relevant contraindications, and viral shedding with transmission precautions for close contacts and healthcare personnel applies.[[10]]
The ASCO systemic therapy for melanoma guideline (2023 update) predates this agent and recommends ipilimumab or ipilimumab-containing regimens, or clinical trial enrollment, after progression on anti–PD-1–based therapy for BRAF wild-type disease (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence).[[17]] No ESMO recommendation addressing vusolimogene oderparepvec was identified in the retrieved literature.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommendation and no clinical trial addresses targeted therapy for TRARG1 alterations, because TRARG1 is not an oncogenic driver or a validated therapeutic target in oncology. TRARG1 (Trafficking Regulator of GLUT4-1) is a metabolic protein that positively regulates insulin-stimulated GLUT4 trafficking and insulin sensitivity in adipocytes; it is a GSK3 substrate situated within the insulin/PI3K/Akt signaling network, and the literature on it concerns glucose metabolism and insulin resistance, not cancer therapy.[[1]] No retrieved guideline or trial evaluates TRARG1-directed therapy, and no biomarker-selection role for TRARG1 appears in precision-oncology sequencing frameworks.[[2]]
A likely source of confusion: TARG1 vs. TRARG1. These are distinct genes with similar names, and only the latter resembles the query:
[[1]][[3]][[4]][[5]]
Even TARG1 has only preclinical cancer data, not guideline or trial-level evidence. Reported findings include: TARG1-deficient cells show heightened sensitivity to MEK1/2 inhibition and reduced EGFR expression, suggesting a hypothetical role as a target to augment MEK inhibitor efficacy; and TARG1 is altered in roughly 1% of cancers per cBioPortal, with a proposed synthetic-lethal strategy using[[5]] the bacterial genotoxin DarT to selectively kill TARG1-deficient cells.[[3]] These are laboratory concepts without any clinical trial or guideline endorsement.
If the intended target was a differently named gene, note that distinct entities such as TRG (T-cell receptor gamma) fusions are recognized oncogenic rearrangements in T-ALL and B-ALL, and TRAF-family genetic alterations have proposed therapeutic rationale across multiple tumor types — but none of these correspond to "TRARG1," and none carry NCCN/ASCO/ESMO targeted-therapy recommendations either.[[6]][[7]]
If you can confirm the exact gene, mutation, or tumor type of interest, a more targeted search of actionable alterations and matched guideline recommendations can be performed.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline addresses TRARG1, and no TRARG1-selected clinical trial was identified in the retrieved literature. TRARG1 is not among the biomarkers any of these societies recommend testing for, and no approved or investigational agent targets it. The NCCN NSCLC biomarker list — EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, NTRK1/2/3, MET exon 14 skipping, RET, ERBB2 (HER2), NRG1, plus HER2 and c-Met IHC and PD-L1 — does not include it, nor does the NCCN emerging-biomarker table (high-level MET amplification, FGFR mutations/fusions, KRAS G12, G13, Q61 mutations).[[1]]
What TRARG1 is
TRARG1 (trafficking regulator of GLUT4-1), formerly named TUSC5, encodes an adipocyte- and peripheral-nerve-enriched protein localized to GLUT4 storage vesicles. It positively regulates insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, is a PPARγ target required for full thiazolidinedione effect, and is a GSK3 substrate within the insulin signaling network.[[2]][[3]][[4]] Knockout mice show impaired glucose disposal, and expression predicts glucose tolerance in obese individuals independent of body weight.[[4]] The "tumor suppressor candidate 5" designation is a legacy name from positional work; the characterized biology is metabolic, and no validated oncogenic driver or tumor-suppressor function supporting a therapeutic strategy has been established in the retrieved literature.
Likely sources of confusion
[[2]][[3]][[4]][[5]][[6]][[7]][[8]][[9]]
The TARG1 confusion is the one most likely to arise clinically. PARG inhibitors are advancing — IDE161 holds FDA fast-track designation for platinum-resistant BRCA1/2-mutant ovarian cancer and HR+/HER2-negative breast cancer, with ETX-19477, XNW29016, and others in development — but enrollment in these programs is selected on HRD/BRCA status and replication-stress phenotypes, not on TARG1 status.[[6]][[10]][[11]][[12]] TARG1 remains a preclinical candidate biomarker only.
Practical interpretation of a TRARG1 finding on an NGS report
The appropriate handling depends on the alteration class, which should be confirmed before concluding it is non-actionable:
- A TRARG1 fusion requires inspection of the partner and reading frame. If TRARG1 is the 5′ partner to a retained ALK, RET, ROS1, or NTRK kinase domain, the actionability derives from the kinase, and NCCN-directed targeted therapy applies.[[1]]
- A single-nucleotide variant or indel in TRARG1 has no established predictive value. NCCN states that any variant classified as a VUS should not be used as a basis for targeted therapy selection, even in a gene in which other variants are clinically actionable.[[1]]
- Copy-number change or expression-level change likewise has no established therapeutic correlate in the retrieved literature.
Treatment should be driven by validated drivers for the tumor type and by established tumor-agnostic markers (MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-high, NTRK1/2/3 fusions, BRAF V600E, RET fusions). ASCO guidelines recommend that for tumors with actionable alterations lacking approved biomarker-linked therapy, clinical trial participation be encouraged after weighing expected efficacy of standard-of-care options (strong recommendation), and emphasize that biologic plausibility alone — absent genomic biomarker-selected clinical or high-level preclinical data — is insufficient to justify a matched agent.[[13]] This standard is not met for TRARG1. Notably, even among NCCN-endorsed genome-targeted recommendations, only about one-eighth were rated as offering high clinical benefit by combined ESCAT/ESMO-MCBS assessment, underscoring how high the bar is for a gene with no clinical dataset at all.[[14]]

A.text: 94d1", "kind": "search", "label": "Searching published medical literature, guidelines, FDA, CDC, and more", "id": "searchmedicalliterature", "active": true, "children": [], "paragraphindex": 0, "metadata": {}, "queries": []}, {"callid": "d09b4b6b-b3aa-4650-bc44-722864820f5f", "kind": "search", "label": "Searching full-text sources from NEJM, JAMA, Nature, NCCN, Cochrane, Wiley, and more", "id": "searchmedicalliterature", "active": true, "children": [], "paragraphindex": 0, "metadata": {}, "queries": []}], "done": true, "summary": "Analyzed query, searched for evidence"} No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends targeted therapy for CLCN3P1 alterations, and no clinical trial has used CLCN3P1 as a selection biomarker or therapeutic target. CLCN3P1 is a pseudogene — a transcribed, non-protein-coding copy of CLCN3 (chloride voltage-gated channel 3). It does not appear in any actionable-biomarker table in the NCCN guidelines, including the NSCLC Principles of Biomarker Analysis and Biomarker-Directed Therapy sections and the Emerging Biomarkers table, the Breast Cancer targeted therapy/biomarker table (BINV-Q-7), or the Biliary Tract Cancers targeted therapy principles (BIL-C-3).[[1]][[2]][[3]] It carries no ESCAT tier in the retrieved literature and is not among the biomarkers with FDA-approved genome-targeted therapies.[[4]][[5]] Why it is not actionable - It is a pseudogene, not a druggable protein-coding driver. Pseudogenes can be transcriptionally active and biologically relevant — including as competing endogenous RNAs, prognostic markers, and candidate future targets — but this remains preclinical/correlative work, with no pseudogene currently established as a treatment-selection biomarker.[[6]][[7]][[8]] - ASCO guidelines require both functional and clinical evidence. The ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion on somatic genomic testing states that clinical decision-making should incorporate the known or predicted impact of an alteration on protein expression or function and clinical data on the efficacy of targeting it (strength: strong). Neither element exists for CLCN3P1. The same PCO recommends strongly against off-label, off-study use of genomic biomarker-linked therapies when a clinical trial is available or without clinical evidence of meaningful efficacy.[[9]] - Most alterations on a sequencing report are passengers. ASCO explicitly notes that the majority of detected alterations have no impact on cancer development, and that presence of an alteration in a gene does not imply drug sensitivity.[[9]] Handling the finding on an NGS report Verify the call with the reporting laboratory before acting on it in any way. Pseudogenes share high sequence homology with their parent genes, so read mismapping is a recognized source of spurious variant calls; a CLCN3P1 call may be analytically real yet still clinically non-actionable, and the distinction should come from the lab rather than be assumed. NCCN emphasizes knowing the spectrum of alterations a given assay does and does not interrogate, and distinguishing an informative result from a null result in which only passenger alterations are reported.[[1]] The parent gene CLCN3 (ClC-3) Evidence here is entirely preclinical. ClC-3 overexpression has been associated with proliferation and cell-cycle progression in [nasopharyngeal carcinoma](/rare-disease/nasopharyngeal-carcinoma), migration/invasion and poor prognosis in cerv[[10]][[11]]ical squamous carcinoma, metastasis via membrane ruffling with poor survival across tumor types, progression in lung adenocarcinoma through an HNRNPK/CLCN3 axis, and multidrug resistance through NF-κB–dependent P-glycoprotein upregulation and vesicular acidification.[[12]][[13]][[14]][[15]][[16]] Knockdown sensitizes glioma cells to cisplatin.[[17]][[18]] The channel modulators used in these studies (NPPB, tamoxifen, chlorotoxin) are not selective ClC-3 inhibitors in this context, and none of this constitutes a clinically validated CLCN3-directed therapy. What to pursue instead Re-review the report for genuinely actionable findings, including the tumor-agnostic biomarkers with FDA approvals: MSI-H/dMMR (pembrolizumab, dostarlimab), TMB-H ≥10 mut/Mb (pembrolizumab), NTRK1/2/3 fusions (larotrectinib, entrectinib, repotrectinib), RET fusions (selpercatinib), BRAF V600E (dabrafenib/trametinib), and HER2-positive (IHC 3+) solid tumors after prior systemic therapy (fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki, accelerated approval).[[19]][[20]][[21]] Beyond that, molecular tumor board review and trial matching are the appropriate route; molecular tumor board discussion measurably increases the rate of genomics-informed therapy changes.[[22]][[23]] Would you like to explore how variants of unknown significance on CGP reports should be triaged and documented?

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommendation or clinical trial addresses targeted therapy for CLCN3P1 alterations, and none was identified in the retrieved literature. CLCN3P1 (chloride voltage-gated channel 3 pseudogene 1) is a processed pseudogene of the CLCN3 gene; it encodes no functional protein and is not a recognized oncogenic driver or actionable biomarker in any professional-society guideline or interventional trial. It does not appear among the ~50 driver alterations underlying the 411 NCCN genome-targeted recommendations catalogued in the most recent cross-sectional analysis of guideline-endorsed molecular targets.[[1]]
Context on the parent gene (CLCN3), which is also not guideline-actionable. The relevant cancer literature concerns the protein-coding gene CLCN3 (ClC-3), not the pseudogene. Even for CLCN3, the evidence is entirely preclinical and observational — there is no approved targeted agent, guideline recommendation, or registered targeted-therapy trial:
- Multidrug resistance: ClC-3 is overexpressed in P-glycoprotein–dependent resistant lung (A549/Taxol) and breast (MCF-7/DOX) cancer cell lines and drives resistance by upregulating MDR1/P-gp via NF-κB signaling, suggesting it as a candidate target to overcome chemoresistance — a laboratory hypothesis only.[[2]]
- Invasion/metastasis and prognosis: Cytoplasmic ClC-3 promotes membrane ruffling and metastasis and correlates with poor survival; it is upregulated in cervical squamous cell carcinoma, where it drives migration/invasion via PI3K/Akt/mTOR–MMP-9 and associates with worse prognosis; and it facilitates lung adenocarcinoma progression through an HNRNPK/CLCN3 axis.[[3]][[4]][[5]][[6]]
- Cell-cycle regulation: ClC-3 promotes [nasopharyngeal carcinoma](/rare-disease/nasopharyngeal-carcinoma) proliferation by upregulating cyclin D1–CDK4/6 and suppressing p21/p27.[[7]]
These reports consistently frame ClC-3 as a potential prognostic biomarker and investigational therapeutic target, but none has advanced to a targeted agent or any guideline/trial endorsement.[[2]][[3]][[5]]
Practical implication. If CLCN3P1 (or a CLCN3 alteration) is appearing on a tumor molecular profiling report, it should be regarded as a variant of uncertain/no established clinical significance for therapy selection rather than an actionable finding. Standard-of-care treatment should be directed by the tumor's histology and by validated, guideline-endorsed biomarkers.
